places.name: Los Angeles River
places.text: The channel beside the freeway is the Los Angeles River. Most of it was lined with concrete after the deadly flood of 1938, but in this 11-mile stretch, the Glendale Narrows, the groundwater sits so high that the bottom was left unpaved. That is why willows, reeds and sandbars grow right in the river.
places.more: The Tongva people, whose homeland this is, called the river Paayme Paxaayt, the West River, and had villages along this stretch. Birdwatchers here count great blue herons, snowy and great egrets, black-crowned night herons, cormorants and even American white pelicans. Steelhead trout swam here before the concrete came, and fishing is still legal all year. A 7.4-mile bike and walking path follows the river, much of it right beside the freeway. In 2013 part of the Narrows opened for summer recreation, and by 2019 kayaking on the river had become common.
places.spot: Look for white egrets or gray herons standing in the shallow water.

places.name: Griffith Park
places.text: The brushy hills west of the freeway are Griffith Park, more than 4,000 acres of chaparral and parkland that the city calls the largest urban-wilderness municipal park in the United States. On December 16, 1896, Griffith J. Griffith gave the first 3,015 acres to the people of Los Angeles as a Christmas gift.
places.more: Griffith had bought Rancho Los Feliz in 1882 and leased part of it for an ostrich farm, since ostrich feathers decorated women's hats. The city's zoo opened on the old ostrich farm in 1912, and when it closed in 1966 some empty enclosures were left standing with picnic tables inside, so people now picnic in the old cages. Griffith's gift came with a wish that the park be open to all, where neither race, creed nor color should be excluded. From 2012 to 2022, a mountain lion known as P-22 made these hills his home. The observatory, the Greek Theatre and trails to the Hollywood Sign are all inside the park.
places.spot: Look for steep, brushy hills rising west of the freeway.

places.name: Zoo, Autry and Travel Town
places.text: Three family stops sit along the north side of Griffith Park: the Los Angeles Zoo, the Autry Museum of the American West, and Travel Town, a railroad museum with 43 full-size engines, cars and other rolling stock. Actor Gene Autry founded his museum of the West here in 1988.
places.more: The zoo's parking lot, the Autry and the freeway interchange here all sit on the old Griffith Park Aerodrome, an airfield used from 1912 until 1939 by aviation pioneers such as Glenn Martin, Bill Boeing and Donald Douglas. After World War II it became Rodger Young Village, 750 Quonset huts built in about two months for returning veterans and their families, and at its peak more than 5,000 people lived there. Travel Town opened in 1952 on land used as an internment camp during World War II, and its first locomotives were left open for children to climb. After the last wild California condors were captured in 1987, the Los Angeles Zoo was one of two places where the survivors were bred.
places.wiki: Autry Museum of the American West

places.name: Grand Central Air Terminal
places.text: Just east of the freeway stands the 1928 terminal building of Grand Central Airport, once a major gateway to Los Angeles by air. In July 1929 it became the western end of the Lindbergh Line, a 48-hour coast-to-coast trip with planes by day and trains by night. The old runway is now a city street, Grand Central Avenue.
places.more: The terminal opened with fanfare on February 22, 1929, designed like a classic railroad station in Spanish and Art Deco styles. Howard Hughes built his record-setting H-1 racer in a small building on Air Way in 1935. In 1933, Albert Forsythe and Charles Anderson landed here on the first round-trip flight across the country by Black pilots. During World War II the government camouflaged the field and trained pilots on it. Walt Disney bought much of the land in 1961 for the designers who became Walt Disney Imagineering, and Disney restored the terminal between 2012 and 2014.

places.name: Verdugo Mountains
places.text: The rocky range rising east of the freeway is the Verdugo Mountains, topping out at 3,126 feet. They are named for José María Verdugo, a Spanish soldier who came north with the 1769 expedition and in 1784 received Rancho San Rafael, about 36,000 acres that now hold Glendale and Burbank.
places.more: Verdugo retired from the army in 1798 to ranch full time, and he soon had nearly 2,000 head of cattle. His heirs later lost much of the land to mortgages and foreclosures. A dentist named David Burbank bought the western part in 1867 to raise sheep and wheat, and the city of Burbank carries his name. In 1871 a lawsuit called the Great Partition split the rancho among 28 people. One peak in the range is now named Tongva Peak, honoring the Tongva people, whose homeland this is and whose villages stood beside springs in its canyons.
places.spot: Look for antenna towers standing on the rocky peaks.

places.name: Lockheed's hidden factory
places.text: During World War II, Lockheed's aircraft factory beside the Burbank airport was disguised from the air. It was covered with a huge painted tarp showing a quiet country neighborhood, with rubber cars and hundreds of fake trees made of chicken wire and feathers. Lockheed and its Vega company built 19,278 planes during the war.
places.more: Lockheed bought the airport in 1940 and ran it as Lockheed Air Terminal, and the field has gone by at least six names, today Hollywood Burbank Airport. In 1943 Lockheed secretly began a jet fighter here, and its secret design shop took the nickname Skunk Works from the Li'l Abner comic strip. That team went on to create the U-2 spy plane, the SR-71 Blackbird and the F-117 stealth fighter. Aerospace work in Burbank ended in 1992. A shopping center on Empire Avenue now covers part of the old Skunk Works site.

places.name: Sun Valley's thorny name
places.text: Long before it was Sun Valley, this was Wixánga, a Fernandeño Tongva village whose name means something like place of the thorns, for the prickly pear cactus growing here. The Spanish name, Cañada de las Tunas, carried the same idea and survives in nearby La Tuna Canyon. Later the area was called Roscoe, and in 1950 residents chose the name Sun Valley.
places.more: The Southern Pacific built its line through the east end of the valley by 1876, linking Southern and Northern California, and a general store here served as post office and water stop. The name Roscoe reportedly came from a railroad crew member. In the 1920s developers, including filmmaker Cecil B. DeMille, laid out a tract called Fernangeles, a blend of San Fernando and Los Angeles. Sitting at the foot of the Verdugo Mountains, the neighborhood is prone to flash floods. Nearby Tujunga Wash, whose name comes from a Tongva word meaning old woman's place, is usually dry and carries much water only during and after storms.

places.name: When the valley grew wheat
places.text: In 1874, J. B. Lankershim and Isaac Van Nuys began dry-farming wheat across the southern half of the San Fernando Valley. By 1876 the valley was the biggest wheat-growing area in Los Angeles County, and that year they sent the first wheat shipment from San Pedro Harbor to Europe.
places.more: Droughts in the 1860s and 1870s showed how badly valley farmers needed a steady water supply. When Los Angeles Aqueduct water arrived after 1913, farms switched from wheat to irrigated crops: corn, beans, squash and cotton, orchards of apricots, persimmons and walnuts, and big groves of oranges and lemons. In Pacoima, growers raised olives, peaches, apricots, oranges and lemons, poultry ranches multiplied, and thoroughbred horses were raised. After World War II the valley's population grew fivefold in 15 years, and suburbs replaced nearly all the farms, leaving only a few groves.

places.name: Pacoima, Ritchie Valens' hometown
places.text: Pacoima takes its name from Pakoinga, the name of a Native village here meaning entrance; Spanish ears heard its ng sound as an m. It is also the hometown of Ritchie Valens, born Richard Valenzuela here in 1941, who turned the Mexican folk song La Bamba into a rock and roll hit in 1958.
places.more: As a student at Pacoima Junior High, Valens brought his guitar to school and sang for friends on the bleachers. On December 10, 1958, he came back to play a concert there, released after his death as his only recorded live performance. He died at 17 in a February 1959 plane crash in Iowa along with Buddy Holly. His La Bamba is preserved in the National Recording Registry, and the stretch of I-5 between the 170 and 118 freeways is named the Ritchie Valens Memorial Highway. After World War II, Pacoima became the center of African American life in the San Fernando Valley, because racial covenants kept Black families out of many other neighborhoods.

places.name: Mission San Fernando
places.text: Mission San Fernando Rey de España was founded on September 8, 1797, the 17th of California's 21 missions, at a place called Achooykomenga. Its convento, a two-story building 243 feet long with four-foot-thick adobe walls and a row of 20 arches, took until 1822 to finish and is often called the largest adobe building in California. The mission gave its name to the San Fernando Valley.
places.more: Native people of the mission, Fernandeño Tongva, Tataviam and Ventureño Chumash among them, tended more than 32,000 grapevines, and at its peak the mission made about 2,000 gallons of wine. Life here was hard: of 1,367 Native children baptized at San Fernando, 965 died in childhood, and some people ran away. In 1920 a 100-pound Russian bell, cast on Kodiak Island in Alaska in 1796, turned up in a nearby orange grove, and no one knows how it got here. The 1971 earthquake badly damaged the church, which was rebuilt by 1974. Comedian Bob Hope is buried in the mission's memorial garden.
places.wiki: Mission San Fernando Rey de España

places.name: The dam that almost failed
places.text: The reservoirs just west of the freeway once supplied about 80 percent of Los Angeles' water. When the San Fernando earthquake struck on February 9, 1971, part of the Lower Van Norman Dam slid into its reservoir, leaving only about 5 feet of dam above the water. Eighty thousand people living below it were evacuated for days.
places.more: The dam was built largely of hydraulic fill, and the shaking liquefied part of it. Luckily the reservoir was only about half full. Crews drained it as fast as the damaged outlets allowed, lowering it 13.5 feet in three and a half days. It was later estimated that a failure could have killed 123,400 people. The old dams were retired, a new Los Angeles Dam was built between them in a more stable spot, and the near miss changed how engineers judge earthquake safety at dams.

places.name: Sylmar's sea of olives
places.text: Sylmar's name, adopted in 1893, joins Latin words for forest and sea, for the sea of olive trees that covered these slopes. In 1894 up to 1,700 acres were planted, and by 1906 the groves were said to be the largest olive grove in the world. Today Sylmar is a suburb, the northernmost neighborhood in Los Angeles.
places.more: Sylmar's olives trace back to Mission San Fernando, which tended about 70 acres of olive trees and crushed the fruit for oil. The Los Angeles Olive Growers Association planted the foothills in the 1890s, planning about a hundred trees to an acre. In the early 1900s, about 300 Japanese workers picked the olives each season and lived in a village of tents. In 1927 the packing plant employed some 500 people in its busiest season. In 1938 the company put its land up for sale, still planted in olives, lemons, oranges and figs.

places.name: Power from the Columbia River
places.text: Near the freeway sits the Sylmar Converter Station, the south end of the Pacific DC Intertie, a power line that runs 846 miles from the Columbia River near The Dalles, Oregon. The line carries direct current, and this station turns it into the alternating current Los Angeles uses, up to 3,100 megawatts.
places.more: The intertie was completed in 1970 to bring cheaper hydroelectric power from dams on the Columbia River, and at the time it was estimated to save Los Angeles customers about 600,000 dollars a day. That is enough power for two to three million Los Angeles households. It takes advantage of opposite seasons: the Northwest uses the most power for heating in winter, while Southern California peaks with summer air conditioning. The 1971 earthquake damaged the station, and in 1989 it expanded onto a field east of the highway.

places.name: Los Angeles Aqueduct Cascades
places.text: On the hillside beside the freeway, water from the eastern Sierra Nevada tumbles down the Cascades, the end of the Los Angeles Aqueduct. When the first water arrived on November 5, 1913, chief engineer William Mulholland said, "There it is. Take it." The original aqueduct runs 233 miles and moves its water by gravity alone.
places.more: Building it took thousands of workers and 164 tunnels, a job compared to the Panama Canal. The water comes from the Owens Valley, homeland of the Paiute people, where the diversions ended most farming and devastated Owens Lake. Because the city could not sell aqueduct water outside its limits, several San Fernando Valley farm towns voted to join Los Angeles in 1915. An extension finished in 1940 moved the system's northernmost intake to near Tioga Pass, so water can travel 338 miles to reach the Cascades.
places.spot: Look for a long concrete water staircase running down the hillside.

places.name: Newhall Pass Interchange
places.text: This tangle of ramps, where I-5 meets the Antelope Valley Freeway, is the Newhall Pass interchange, and parts of I-5 here are up to 21 lanes wide. Earthquakes knocked down ramps here twice, in 1971 and again in 1994. Officially it is the Clarence Wayne Dean Memorial Interchange, named for a police officer killed in the 1994 collapse.
places.more: On January 17, 1994, Los Angeles police motorcycle officer Clarence Wayne Dean was riding to work when he could not stop in time and fell from a broken ramp. Both quakes dropped ramps onto the lanes below in nearly the same way. After each one, the structures were rebuilt with stronger reinforcement. The separate truck lanes that loop around the main lanes are the original four-lane freeway, built as US 99. The main lanes follow a bypass through Weldon and Gavin canyons, built by 1930 to avoid Newhall Pass itself.
places.spot: Look for flyover ramps curving high above the lanes on tall columns.

places.name: Oak of the Golden Dream
places.text: In Placerita Canyon, a few miles east, Francisco López made what the state's landmark plaque calls California's first authenticated gold discovery, on March 9, 1842. Gathering wild onions near an oak tree, he found gold flakes clinging to the onion roots. That was six years before the famous strike at Sutter's Mill, and the tree is now called the Oak of the Golden Dream.
places.more: Local legend says López napped under the oak and dreamed he was floating on a pool of gold before he pulled the onions. In fact he had studied mineralogy at the University of Mexico and was searching for gold. About 2,000 people, mostly from the Mexican state of Sonora, came to mine the area by panning, sluicing and dry washing. During the Mexican-American War, the rancho's owner destroyed the mine to keep it from the United States. The oak stands in Placerita Canyon, homeland of the Tataviam people, where a rare clear oil still seeps beside a trail.

places.name: Beale's Cut
places.text: Before tunnels and freeways, stagecoaches crossed this pass through Beale's Cut, a slot dug through the mountain with picks and shovels and eventually deepened to 90 feet. Edward Beale, who won the right to collect tolls here in 1863, used Chinese immigrant workers to do most of the digging. Butterfield Overland Mail coaches running to San Francisco used the cut.
places.more: Silent movie makers loved the cut. In a 1923 film by director John Ford, cowboy star Tom Mix is filmed leaping across it, though film historians have long debated whether Mix, a stuntman or a camera trick made the jump. The Newhall auto tunnel replaced the cut in 1910, and the 1994 earthquake collapsed part of the cut, leaving it about 30 feet deep. Under the same mountain, more than 1,500 mostly Chinese laborers dug the 6,940-foot San Fernando railroad tunnel in 1875 and 1876. Crews digging from both ends met only half an inch out of line, and trains still use the tunnel today.

places.name: William S. Hart Park
places.text: In Newhall, the ranch of silent film cowboy William S. Hart is now a 265-acre park with his Spanish-style mansion, trails and a barnyard of farm animals. Hart left it to Los Angeles County when he died in 1946. Before he died he said, "When I was making pictures, the people gave me their nickels, dimes, and quarters. When I am gone, I want them to have my home."
places.more: Hart was one of the most popular movie stars of the late 1910s, known for gritty westerns and a pinto horse named Fritz. He came to the movies from the Shakespearean stage in 1914, when he was nearly 50. After his 1925 film Tumbleweeds, he retired to this ranch, called La Loma de los Vientos, and made no more feature films. The mansion holds his collection, including Native American artifacts and works by the artist Charles Russell. The City of Santa Clarita took over the park and museum from the county in 2025 and offers guided house tours.

places.name: Pico Number 4 oil well
places.text: Up Pico Canyon, west of the freeway, Well Number 4 struck oil on September 26, 1876, and became the first commercially successful oil well in the western United States. It kept producing for 114 years until it was capped in 1990, and it is often called the longest continuously operating oil well in the world.
places.more: Driller Charles Mentry built his drill stem from old railroad car axles, and in 1877 oil spurted to the top of the 65-foot derrick. He then laid California's first oil pipeline, to a refinery in Newhall that is called the oldest existing refinery in the world. The boom town of Mentryville grew up just down the canyon, with a schoolhouse and a gas-lit tennis court but no bar, because Mentry reportedly banned drinking and swearing. Long before, the Tataviam and Tongva people used oil from seeps here as medicine.

places.name: Tataviam homeland
places.text: The Santa Clarita Valley is considered the heart of the homeland of the Tataviam people, a name that means people on the south slope in the neighboring Kitanemuk language. They lived in about 20 villages in and around the valley, with summer and winter settlements, and harvested yucca and juniper berries. Their tribe today, the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians, is governed from San Fernando.
places.more: When the Portolá expedition camped by the river here in August 1769, its members found a large village and watched a wedding celebration. By 1810 nearly all the Tataviam had been baptized at Mission San Fernando, and many died of diseases the newcomers brought. When the missions were shut down, their land here was supposed to be returned to the Tataviam, but in 1839 the governor granted it to his friend Antonio del Valle instead. The tribe is not federally recognized. Its land conservancy, founded in 2018, has had more than 550 acres of ancestral land returned.

places.name: Santa Clara River
places.text: The Santa Clara River, which passes under the freeway near Magic Mountain Parkway, runs 83 miles to the Pacific and is one of the least altered rivers in Southern California. Here its bed is dry most of the year. Spanish explorers named it on August 9, 1769, for Saint Clare of Assisi, and the valley later became known as little Santa Clara, Santa Clarita, to tell it apart from Santa Clara in Northern California.
places.more: Its watershed is the homeland of the Tataviam people in the north and the Chumash people in the south. The river still shelters threatened wildlife. Among them are a small fish called the unarmored threespine stickleback, steelhead trout, southwestern pond turtles and least Bell's vireos. Before 1940 its steelhead run was one of the largest in Southern California.

places.name: Six Flags Magic Mountain
places.text: The roller coaster tracks twisting over the hills west of the freeway belong to Six Flags Magic Mountain, which opened on May 29, 1971. In 2022 it became the first amusement park to offer 20 roller coasters. Several have closed since, but it still has one of the biggest collections of coasters anywhere.
places.more: The park was built by the Newhall Land and Farming Company in partnership with Sea World's founder. It took its name from Magic Mountain, a peak east of the Santa Clarita Valley. When it opened, the valley was so remote that Greyhound ran buses to it from Los Angeles and Northern California. Its Colossus coaster of 1978 was then the fastest and largest dual-track wooden coaster in the world. Six Flags bought the park in 1979, and it had permission to use Looney Tunes characters from its very first season.
places.spot: Look for roller coaster tracks looping over the hills west of the freeway.

places.name: The Death Valley rescue
places.text: Near where Highway 126 meets the freeway stood the adobe headquarters of Rancho San Francisco, first built about 1804 as a granary for Mission San Fernando. In January 1850, William Lewis Manly and John Rogers reached it and got supplies and animals to rescue their gold-seeking emigrant party, stranded and starving in Death Valley about 250 miles northeast.
places.more: The rancho's 48,612 acres were granted in 1839 to Antonio del Valle, and much of today's Santa Clarita lies inside its old boundaries. After floods and droughts, the family sold most of it in 1862, and it eventually passed to Henry Newhall, who paid 2 dollars an acre. Newhall gave the Southern Pacific a right of way, and the railroad named its new town Newhall. He named the first station on the line Saugus, after his hometown in Massachusetts. In 1936 his grandson-in-law, Atholl McBean, found oil on the property.

places.name: St. Francis Dam disaster
places.text: Just before midnight on March 12, 1928, the St. Francis Dam failed in San Francisquito Canyon, about 10 miles north of Santa Clarita. The flood tore down the canyon and along the Santa Clara River to the sea, killing at least 431 people. It is considered the second-deadliest dam failure in American history.
places.more: The dam was part of the Los Angeles Aqueduct system, designed and built under William Mulholland, and its failure ended his career. Around one in the morning the water, still 55 feet high, swept west along the river past this junction. It flooded at least four miles of the state's main north-south highway and washed away the settlement of Castaic Junction. Downstream, 84 workers died at a power company construction camp. The flood reached the ocean south of Ventura around 5:30 in the morning, nearly two miles wide. In 2019, Congress made the site the Saint Francis Dam Disaster National Monument.

places.name: Val Verde, the Black Palm Springs
places.text: In the hills west of the freeway, Black investors led by Sidney Dones founded a resort community in 1924, when African Americans were often barred from public beaches and pools. It became known as the Black Palm Springs, and Ella Fitzgerald and Lena Horne appeared there. Today it is the community of Val Verde, Spanish for green valley.
places.more: It began as Eureka Villa, on ranch land whose white owner, Laura Janes, had opened it to African Americans in the 1910s. Families bought small lots to build vacation homes, and in 1927 landowners donated 53 acres that became Val Verde Park. In 1939 actress Hattie McDaniel presided over the cornerstone ceremony for its Olympic swimming pool; repaired and shortened after the 1994 earthquake, the pool still opens from late spring to early fall. Racism followed even here: in 1964 the Ku Klux Klan burned the home of a Black World War II veteran. After civil rights reforms in the 1960s opened other neighborhoods, many families moved away.

places.name: Castaic Lake and its name
places.text: Castaic takes its name from the Chumash word Kaštiq, meaning the eye. Above the town, Castaic Dam, finished in 1973, rises 340 feet and stretches nearly a mile, holding Castaic Lake at the end of the West Branch of the California Aqueduct. Water from Northern California rests here before flowing on to millions of people around Los Angeles.
places.more: The Spanish spelled the name Castéc, and it first described a canyon on the trail to an old Chumash camp at Castac Lake, near Lebec, which carries the same name. Modern Castaic began in 1887 as a Southern Pacific siding called Castaic Junction. When snow closes the pass, a gate in the freeway median just north of Lake Hughes Road lets drivers turn around. Fans of the Mighty Morphin Power Rangers may know the lake, because many of the show's action scenes were filmed here. In January 2025 the Hughes Fire burned 10,425 acres east of the lake, and at its height more than 30,000 people were under evacuation orders.

places.name: Five Mile Grade crossover
places.text: On the Five Mile Grade north of Castaic, the two sides of the freeway trade places, so for about 5 miles traffic keeps to the left. When I-5 was rebuilt in the 1960s, engineers put the uphill and downhill lanes on separate hillsides, and the downhill lanes got a gentler grade to cut down on runaway trucks.
places.more: One set of lanes is the old four-lane Ridge Route Alternate, widened between 1948 and 1952. The other was added to the east, next to the original 1915 Ridge Route. Two bridges carry traffic across to the left side and back again. The plan began as a six-lane freeway and grew to eight lanes before the work was finished in 1970. The north end of the grade marks the edge of the Angeles National Forest.
places.spot: Look for the other direction's lanes running on a separate hillside.

places.name: The old Ridge Route
places.text: East of the freeway, the original Ridge Route of 1915 winds along the ridgetops from Castaic toward Gorman. It was the first paved highway linking Los Angeles directly with the San Joaquin Valley, and between Castaic and Gorman its 697 turns added up to about 97 complete circles in 36 miles. Between Castaic and Quail Lake the speed limit was 15 miles an hour.
places.more: Roadhouses served travelers along the way, including the National Forest Inn, the Tumble Inn and Sandberg's Summit Hotel, a log lodge from 1914 near the road's highest point, Liebre Summit, 4,233 feet. The road was paved with concrete by 1921 and bypassed in 1933. About 17.6 miles of it in the Angeles National Forest went on the National Register of Historic Places in 1997, thanks largely to retired engineer Harrison Scott. Much of it is now closed to cars. The Templin Highway exit takes its name from a road renamed in 1967 for county highway commissioner Newton Templin.

places.name: Highway 99 under the lake
places.text: Beneath Pyramid Lake lies a drowned highway. In 1933 the three-lane Ridge Route Alternate, later US 99, opened through the canyon of Piru Creek, with a middle lane that drivers in both directions used for passing, nicknamed the suicide lane. After Pyramid Dam was finished, rising water covered the old road, and by 1972 it was fully under the lake.
places.more: The lake takes its name from Pyramid Rock, a pointed chunk of mountain left behind in 1932 when road builders cut through a ridge for the highway. The rock still stands in front of the dam. US 99 was called the Main Street of California, and in the 1930s Dust Bowl migrant farm workers traveled it across the state. Today a piece of the old road at the lake's north end serves as a boat ramp, and the dam stands 386 feet high.

places.name: Vista del Lago
places.text: The Vista del Lago Visitors Center, off its own exit, sits above Pyramid Lake with an outdoor overlook and exhibits from the California Department of Water Resources. The lake holds about 180,000 acre-feet of State Water Project water, pumped up from the San Joaquin Valley and over the Tehachapi Mountains.
places.more: From the lake, water drops 1,060 feet through the 7.2-mile Angeles Tunnel, 30 feet across, to the Castaic Power Plant at the upper end of Castaic Lake. The plant makes electricity at times of peak demand, and it can pump water back uphill to store energy. Each of its six main units is rated at 250 megawatts, nearly twice the size of the largest generators at Hoover Dam. Pyramid Lake offers boating, fishing and picnic sites, including five that can be reached only by boat.

places.name: Quail Lake on the fault
places.text: Quail Lake, along Highway 138 east of the freeway, lies in the rift zone of the San Andreas Fault and stores water for the West Branch of the California Aqueduct. Water pumped up to the lake flows by gravity through a pipeline to a power plant at Pyramid Lake. The fault itself slices right through Gorman.
places.more: This part of the San Andreas last broke on January 9, 1857, in one of the largest earthquakes recorded in the United States, about magnitude 7.9. The rupture ran about 225 miles, from Parkfield to Wrightwood, and the ground slipped about 15 feet on average. One of only two deaths reported was a woman in nearby Gorman, killed when an adobe house collapsed. It is often called the last Big One in Southern California, and this section has not had a large quake since. The Pacific Plate moves north past the North American Plate about an inch and a half a year.

places.name: Gorman and its wildflowers
places.text: In spring after a wet winter, California poppies and lupine can blanket the hills around Gorman. People have stopped here for centuries: it was the Tataviam village of Kulshra'jek, a trading crossroads, and a local historian calls it one of the oldest continuously used roadside rest stops in California. In 2005 Gorman had only 15 homes.
places.more: The town is named for James Gorman, who reportedly worked at Fort Tejon as a teamster and herder and in 1867 or 1868 bought the log roadhouse here, which became known as Gorman's Station. Stagecoach drivers changed horses here, using six to pull a coach up the pass from Bakersfield. In 1991 the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude placed 1,760 large yellow umbrellas from the roadsides up the mountainsides around Gorman and Tejon Pass, and closed the show early after a woman was crushed by a windblown umbrella. Next door, Hungry Valley State Vehicular Recreation Area, more than 19,000 acres, offers guided wildflower tours from mid-April through May; its guide notes that poppies close on cloudy, windy days and at night. In June 2024 the Post Fire started beside the freeway near Gorman Post Road and burned more than 15,000 acres.
places.spot: Look for orange California poppies on the hillsides in spring.

places.name: Tejon Pass summit
places.text: Near the top of Tejon Pass, I-5 reaches 4,144 feet, its highest point in California, close to the line between Los Angeles and Kern counties. The pass sits where California's two largest faults, the San Andreas and the Garlock, meet. Tejón is Spanish for badger, though the dead badger behind the name was found in 1806 at a different canyon, about 15 miles northeast.
places.more: Lieutenant Pedro Fages crossed this pass in 1772 and called it Portezuelo de Cortes. Later it was the Castac Pass, then the Fort Tejon Pass, after the Army post down the canyon, and finally just Tejon Pass. Snow and ice close I-5 here an average of three to five times a winter, between October and April. Rather than order chains, the Highway Patrol usually closes the freeway outright, because of the steep grade and the heavy traffic of cars and big rigs.

places.name: Frazier Mountain
places.text: The broad, pine-covered peak west of the pass is Frazier Mountain, 8,017 feet high. To the Chumash people it is Toshololo, the mountain of the east, named for its place east of Mount Pinos and tied to the morning star and the spring equinox. Its English name honors William Frazer, a miner who worked here in the 1850s.
places.more: In 1854, lumber was cut from Frazier Mountain's trees for the new Army post at Fort Tejon. The town of Frazier Park, founded in 1925 on the mountain's north side, took the mountain's name in 1926. In 2023 a store there sold a Powerball ticket worth 1.75 billion dollars. Farther west rises Mount Pinos, 8,847 feet, the highest point in Ventura County, whose summit the Chumash call the center of the world. Mount Pinos is considered home to one of California's most significant populations of birds of prey, and California condors live in the area.
places.spot: Look for a broad, pine-covered mountain rising west of the freeway.

places.name: Castac Lake, the eye
places.text: East of Lebec lies Castac Lake, a natural salty lake that formed about 10,000 years ago when the fan of sediment washed down by Cuddy Creek dammed a valley along the Garlock Fault. The Chumash, Kitanemuk and Yokuts peoples all named it for an eye.
places.more: Several villages stood near its shores, including the Emigdiano Chumash village of Sasau on the north side. In 1772 Pedro Fages named it Salinas de Cortes, and in the late 1800s and early 1900s its bed was sometimes mined for salt when it dried out. The Garlock Fault that shaped it is California's second-longest, running about 160 miles east toward Death Valley. Since 2001, Tejon Ranch has pumped groundwater to keep the lake's level up.

places.name: Tejon Ranch cattle
places.text: The open hills around Lebec are part of Tejon Ranch, more than 270,000 acres and the largest single piece of private land in California. Cattle graze about 250,000 acres of it, up to 12,000 head depending on the season. The ranch says you know winter is over when orange poppies spill across the hills and young calves trail their mothers.
places.more: The ranch grew from four Mexican land grants of the 1840s, which Edward Fitzgerald Beale bought between 1855 and 1866. In 1912 Beale's son sold it to investors led by Los Angeles Times publisher Harry Chandler. A 2008 agreement was designed to protect about 240,000 acres, nearly 90 percent of the ranch, and was called the largest conservation pact in California history. For one development, the company agreed to leave four of five north-facing ridgelines open because California condors feed there. A little less than 6,000 acres grow pistachios, almonds, wine grapes, alfalfa and now olives.
places.spot: Look for cattle grazing on the open hillsides.

places.name: Fort Tejon
places.text: The adobe buildings among the oaks beside the freeway are Fort Tejon, an Army post from 1854 to 1864 on the main route between the Central Valley and Southern California. From 1858 it was the western end of the Army's experiment with camels as pack animals. The soldiers found the camels hardy but temperamental, and they spooked the cavalry's horses.
places.more: Fort Tejon was home to the First U.S. Dragoons until the Civil War, and it was also a stop on the Butterfield Overland Mail. The great 1857 earthquake on the San Andreas Fault badly damaged most of its adobe buildings and became known by the fort's name. Hard history happened here too: in July 1863, after soldiers killed hundreds of Paiute people in the Owens Valley, about 850 survivors were marched to Fort Tejon. Since 1940 the fort has been a state historic park, with restored barracks, 300-year-old valley oaks and living history demonstrations.
places.spot: Look for low adobe buildings under big oak trees beside the freeway.

places.name: Peter Lebeck's oak
places.text: On the fort grounds is the grave of Peter Lebeck, buried under a valley oak in 1837. Someone carved his epitaph into the tree: Peter Lebeck, killed by a X bear, October 17, 1837. Early settlers called grizzlies X bears, probably for a dark pattern on their backs, and he is the earliest known victim of a bear attack in California.
places.more: Almost nothing else is known about him; the Catholic symbol on the carving suggests he may have been a French-Canadian trapper. The oak's bark slowly grew over the letters. In 1890 a group from Bakersfield called the Foxtail Rangers peeled it back and found the inscription printed in reverse on the underside. That piece of bark is now in the museum at Fort Tejon. The nearby town of Lebec is named for him, and in 1915 an 1837 five-franc coin found in the fort's ruins fed legends that he was connected to the French government.

places.name: The Grapevine grade
places.text: This steep stretch through Grapevine Canyon is the Grapevine itself, a 6 percent grade that runs 5 miles and drops about 1,600 feet. Escape ramps branch off the downhill lanes for big rigs whose brakes fail, and in hot weather car engines often overheat on the long uphill lanes.
places.more: The name comes from wild California grapevines: in 1772 Pedro Fages called this canyon Cañada de las Uvas, the canyon of the grapes. On the old road through it, a bend called Dead Man's Curve was the scene of many wrecks. In July 1932, truck driver Jack Klieby steered his gasoline truck off the road to avoid hitting oncoming cars and died when it burst into flames. Work finished in 1935 straightened the worst curves, removing the equivalent of eight complete circles. The old curve can still be seen from Digier Road, west of the freeway.
places.spot: Look for steep escape ramps built for trucks whose brakes fail.

places.name: California's first reservation
places.text: These mountains are ancestral homeland of the Tejon Indian Tribe, a federally recognized tribe of Kitanemuk, Yokuts, Paiute and Chumash people based in Bakersfield. In 1853 they became the site of California's first Indian reservation, the Sebastian, or Tejon, Reservation, which reached from Tejon Canyon west to Grapevine Canyon. The state's historical marker says the number of people living there varied from 500 to 2,000.
places.more: Edward Beale, the federal superintendent of Indian affairs, set it up on a private Mexican land grant. Residents planted wheat, barley and corn, and Tejon Creek watered gardens, vineyards and orchards. Drought, crop disease and settlers' cattle eating the crops wore it down. In April 1864 a Tejon leader, José Pacheco, wrote that he believed the agents kept and sold the provisions meant for his people, while they and their children went hungry. The reservation closed that year. Many people were forced at gunpoint to the new Tule River Reservation near Porterville, while about a hundred stayed on land Beale had bought for his own ranch, which became Tejon Ranch. One Kitanemuk family still lives on the ranch.

zones.label: LA River and Griffith Park
zones.text: The freeway follows the Los Angeles River through the Glendale Narrows, with the brushy hills of Griffith Park on the west side.

zones.label: Burbank and Sun Valley
zones.text: Studios, the airport and the neighborhoods of Glendale, Burbank and Sun Valley spread across the flat east end of the San Fernando Valley, below the rocky Verdugo Mountains.

seasons.winter: Tujunga Wash, a mostly dry riverbed in this part of the valley, usually carries much water only during storms between November and April.

zones.label: North San Fernando Valley
zones.text: Pacoima, Mission Hills and Sylmar fill the north end of the valley, once a land of mission vineyards, wheat and olive groves, with the San Gabriel Mountains rising close by.

seasons.winter: Snow almost never falls on the valley floor, but the mountains of the Angeles National Forest above Sylmar are capped with snow every winter.

zones.label: Newhall Pass and Newhall
zones.text: Newhall Pass, between the San Gabriel and Santa Susana Mountains, links the San Fernando Valley with the Santa Clarita Valley, where Newhall grew up as a railroad and oil town.

seasons.summer: Summer heat in the pass can top 100 degrees.
seasons.winter: Snow is possible here from December to February, but it is quite uncommon.

zones.label: Santa Clarita Valley
zones.text: Planned neighborhoods of Valencia spread along the Santa Clara River, with Magic Mountain's roller coasters on the hills west of the freeway.

seasons.spring: In April and May, chaparral yucca send up flower stalks 3 to 10 feet tall.

zones.label: Castaic and the Five Mile Grade
zones.text: North of Castaic, the long Five Mile Grade leads into the Angeles National Forest, where the freeway crosses the Sierra Pelona Mountains between Castaic Lake and Pyramid Lake.

seasons.winter: Ice and snow sometimes lead the Highway Patrol to close the 40 miles of I-5 between Castaic and Grapevine.

zones.label: Pyramid Lake to Gorman
zones.text: Pyramid Lake fills the canyon of Piru Creek west of the freeway in the Sierra Pelona Mountains, and farther north the land opens into Peace Valley around Gorman.

seasons.spring: From mid-April through May, Hungry Valley near Gorman offers guided wildflower tours.

zones.label: Tejon Pass and Lebec
zones.text: Tejon Pass sits among the open hills of Tejon Ranch around Lebec.

seasons.winter: When snow and ice close the freeway over the pass, the shutdown usually lasts four to six hours, but some closures run longer than a day.
seasons.spring: Spring brings showy wildflower blooms to Tejon Ranch, where several of California's natural regions meet.

zones.label: Grapevine Canyon
zones.text: Grapevine Canyon carries the freeway's long, steep grade past Fort Tejon's centuries-old valley oaks to the southern edge of the San Joaquin Valley.

seasons.fall: Autumn was acorn harvest time for the Kitanemuk people, whose homeland includes these mountains.

trivia.q: In 1896, Griffith J. Griffith gave Los Angeles the first 3,015 acres of Griffith Park as what kind of present?
trivia.why: He gave the land on December 16, 1896, as a Christmas gift to the people of Los Angeles.

trivia.q: During World War II, how was Lockheed's aircraft factory in Burbank hidden from the air?
choices: It was moved into a cave
It was painted to look like a lake
It was covered by a painted tarp showing a neighborhood
It was hidden inside a movie studio
trivia.why: A huge painted tarp, rubber cars and fake trees of chicken wire and feathers made it look like a quiet neighborhood.

trivia.q: Which rock and roll pioneer grew up in Pacoima?
trivia.why: Ritchie Valens was born in Pacoima in 1941 and turned La Bamba into a hit in 1958.

trivia.q: Sylmar's name blends Latin words for which two things?
trivia.why: Sylmar joins Latin words for forest and sea, for the sea of olive trees that once covered it.

trivia.q: What did William Mulholland say when Los Angeles Aqueduct water first arrived in 1913?
trivia.why: He spoke those words at the opening ceremony on November 5, 1913.

trivia.q: In 1842, Francisco López found gold in Placerita Canyon clinging to the roots of what?
trivia.why: He was gathering wild onions near an oak and found gold on their roots, six years before Sutter's Mill.

trivia.q: How long did the Pico Number 4 oil well keep producing before it was capped?
trivia.why: It struck oil in 1876 and was capped in 1990, 114 years later.

trivia.q: Many animated movies hide the code A113 as an inside joke. What was A113?
choices: A classroom at CalArts in Valencia
A license plate on a studio car
trivia.why: A113 is the CalArts classroom where its character animation program began, and alumni slip it into their work as a tribute.

trivia.q: On the Five Mile Grade north of Castaic, what is unusual about I-5?
choices: Traffic keeps to the left side
It runs through a long tunnel
trivia.why: When the freeway was rebuilt in the 1960s, the two directions swapped sides for about 5 miles.

trivia.q: How did Pyramid Lake get its name?
choices: From a pyramid-shaped rock left by road builders
From an ancient pyramid under the water
From the shape of its dam
From an old hotel by the shore
trivia.why: Road builders cut through a ridge for Highway 99 in 1932, leaving Pyramid Rock, which still stands in front of the dam.

trivia.q: Tejon Pass is named after an animal. What does tejón mean in Spanish?
trivia.why: The name came from a dead badger found in 1806 at the mouth of a canyon about 15 miles northeast of today's pass.

trivia.q: Starting in 1858, which unusual animals did the Army test at Fort Tejon?
trivia.why: Fort Tejon was the western end of the Army's experimental Camel Corps.
